title: Riverside Hardware: moving the books to the cloud, preserving records and XBRL
participant_role: Accountant at the accounting firm that keeps the books for RIVERSIDE HARDWARE
judge_role: Owner of RIVERSIDE HARDWARE (two stores), who uses 8-year-old desktop accounting software and keeps paper receipts in boxes

difficulty.rationale: Mostly conceptual with one cost comparison; easier than State.
difficulty.suggested_adjustment: Could be used at District; add a data conversion problem to raise it.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of an accountant at the accounting firm that keeps the books for RIVERSIDE HARDWARE. The owner (judge) of RIVERSIDE HARDWARE wants your advice on modernizing the company's accounting system.

RIVERSIDE HARDWARE is a family owned business with two stores in neighboring towns. The owner (judge) records all transactions in desktop accounting software that was installed eight years ago on a single computer in the back office of the main store. The manager of the second store emails daily sales totals, which are keyed in by hand the next morning. Paper receipts and vendor invoices are kept in boxes in a storage closet, and the data file is copied to a flash drive "whenever someone remembers."

The company's bank recently renewed its line of credit and now requires monthly financial statements within 15 days after the end of each month. The owner (judge) is worried that the current process cannot meet that deadline. A software vendor has offered a cloud accounting subscription, and the owner (judge) has gathered the annual costs of both options.

[Annual cost comparison: see exhibits]

At a recent meeting, a representative of one of the stores' largest suppliers, a public company, mentioned that the supplier files its financial statements using "XBRL." The owner (judge) has never heard the term and wants to know whether it matters to RIVERSIDE HARDWARE.

You must:
- Explain how accounting applications and systems are used in a business like RIVERSIDE HARDWARE
- Compare the costs and benefits of the desktop system and the cloud system
- Recommend ways to preserve the company's automated accounting records
- Identify strategies for getting transaction data into the accounting system
- Explain the nature of XBRL and whether it applies to RIVERSIDE HARDWARE

You will present your recommendations to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's office at the main store. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your recommendations and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: What happens to my data if the cloud company goes out of business?
Is it safe to connect my bank account to the software?

solution.overview: A strong answer shows that the desktop system costs $6,800 a year compared with $5,400 for the cloud system, a saving of $1,400, and adds remote access for both stores, automatic backups and bank feeds. The presenter recommends a backup, security and retention plan, lists ways to automate data entry and explains that XBRL is required for public companies but not for a private business like RIVERSIDE HARDWARE, all in clear, plain language.

answer: Accounting software records transactions in journals and posts them to the general ledger automatically
It produces trial balances, financial statements and aging reports on demand, which helps meet the bank's monthly deadline
Modules handle sales, purchases and payables, inventory, payroll and bank reconciliation
A cloud system can connect to the stores' cash registers and the bank so data flows in without retyping
User access levels let each person see and change only what their job requires
Cloud yearly cost: 450 x 12 = $5,400
The cloud system saves $1,400 a year
Cloud also adds remote access for both stores, automatic updates and backups, and bank feeds
Tradeoffs: it needs reliable internet, the monthly fee never ends, and converting the data takes time
Use automatic backups and follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, on 2 types of media, with 1 copy offsite
Protect access with individual user logins, access levels and multifactor authentication
Scan paper receipts and attach them to the related transactions
Keep records for required periods: generally at least 3 years for tax records, 7 years for some items and at least 4 years for payroll records
Export and archive a full copy of the old desktop data before switching
Bank and credit card feeds bring in transactions every day
Point of sale (POS) integration posts each store's daily sales automatically
Receipt capture apps turn photos of receipts into entries
Vendors can send electronic invoices straight into accounts payable; manual entry is kept for exceptions
Limitations: accounts must be mapped and old data cleaned up during conversion, and imported data still needs review
XBRL (Extensible Business Reporting Language) tags each number in the financial statements so computers can read it
For example, a tag tells software that a number is revenue for a specific company and period
The SEC requires public companies to file using XBRL so investors and regulators can compare data quickly
RIVERSIDE HARDWARE is private, so XBRL is not required, but it shows where financial reporting is heading

judge_question_answers.question: What happens to my data if the cloud company goes out of business?
answer: Choose an established provider and read the contract for data ownership and export rights
Export a full backup of the books regularly (for example monthly) and store it offsite
Reputable providers give notice and export tools if a service ends
The data belongs to the company, and backups let it move to another system

judge_question_answers.question: Is it safe to connect my bank account to the software?
answer: Bank feeds are generally read only: the software can see transactions but cannot move money
Connections use encryption and secure links approved by the bank
Turn on multifactor authentication and limit who has administrator access
Reconcile the bank account every month to catch errors or fraud

key_concepts.definition: Software that records transactions, posts them to the ledger and produces reports and financial statements.
Accounting software run on the provider's servers and used through the internet, paid for with a subscription that includes updates and backups.
A secure connection that imports bank and credit card transactions into the accounting software automatically.
A link between the point of sale (cash register) system and the accounting software that posts daily sales without retyping.
The ways transaction data gets into the accounting system, such as feeds, integrations, scanning apps, electronic invoices and manual entry.
Keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different types of media, with 1 copy stored offsite.
Keeping business records for the required time. Tax records are generally kept at least 3 years and payroll records at least 4 years.
A login that requires two or more proofs of identity, such as a password plus a code sent to a phone.
Moving data from an old system to a new one, which requires mapping accounts and cleaning up errors.
Extensible Business Reporting Language: a tagging language that makes financial statement data machine readable. The SEC requires it for public company filings.

notes: State level because the student must compare two cost options with simple math and explain several technology terms, including XBRL, in plain language. Watch for students who forget to spread the $6,000 replacement over 3 years, who treat the cloud itself as the only backup, or who say RIVERSIDE HARDWARE must file in XBRL.

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the software journalizes and posts to the general ledger automatically, produces statements on demand to meet the bank's 15 day deadline, and uses modules and user access levels, then shows the desktop costs $6,800 a year ($1,200 + $3,600 + $6,000 / 3) against $5,400 for the cloud, a $1,400 saving plus remote access, automatic backups and bank feeds, while naming the tradeoffs (internet, never ending fee, conversion time).
criteria.meets: Describes how accounting software records, posts and reports transactions, and correctly calculates desktop $6,800 against cloud $5,400 a year for a $1,400 saving with at least one added benefit of the cloud.
criteria.below: Gives a general description of accounting software, or compares costs incorrectly, for example forgetting to spread the $6,000 replacement over 3 years and comparing $10,800 with $5,400.
criteria.little: Does not explain what accounting systems do or does not compare the two options with any numbers.

items.label: Describe the nature of Extensible Business Reporting Language (XBRL)

criteria.exceeds: Explains that XBRL tags each number in the financial statements so computers can read it (for example a tag marking a number as revenue for a specific company and period), that the SEC requires it for public companies like the supplier so investors and regulators can compare data quickly, and that RIVERSIDE HARDWARE is private so it is not required but shows where reporting is heading.
criteria.meets: Defines XBRL as a tagging language that makes financial data machine readable, notes the SEC requires it for public companies, and states that RIVERSIDE HARDWARE does not have to use it.
criteria.below: Gives a vague or partly wrong definition of XBRL, or says RIVERSIDE HARDWARE must file in XBRL.
criteria.little: Cannot explain what XBRL is or does not address whether it applies.

criteria.exceeds: Recommends automatic backups using the 3-2-1 rule (3 copies, 2 types of media, 1 offsite), individual logins with access levels and multifactor authentication, scanning paper receipts and attaching them to transactions, retention periods (at least 3 years for tax, 4 years for payroll, 7 years for some items), and exporting a full archive of the old desktop data before switching.
criteria.meets: Recommends regular automatic backups kept offsite, secure user access, scanning receipts, and keeping records for required retention periods.
criteria.below: Mentions backups in general terms only, or treats the cloud itself as the only backup without offsite copies or retention periods.
criteria.little: Gives no plan for preserving records, or accepts the flash drive copy made whenever someone remembers.

criteria.exceeds: Names bank and credit card feeds, point of sale integration that posts each store's daily sales (ending the emailed totals keyed in by hand), receipt capture apps and electronic vendor invoices, keeps manual entry for exceptions, and explains limits such as mapping accounts, cleaning old data during conversion and reviewing imported data.
criteria.meets: Identifies at least three ways to automate data entry, such as bank feeds, POS integration and receipt capture apps, and connects them to removing the second store's manual keying.
criteria.below: Names only one or two strategies without linking them to RIVERSIDE HARDWARE's current process, or ignores the need to review imported data.
criteria.little: Does not identify any way to get data into the system other than typing it in.

items.label: Explain the nature of effective verbal communications

criteria.exceeds: Explains technical terms such as cloud, bank feed, 3-2-1 backup and XBRL in plain language the owner can follow, checks for understanding, and organizes the advice in a logical order ending in a clear recommendation to move to the cloud.
criteria.meets: Speaks clearly and in an organized way, defining most technical terms so a small business owner can understand the recommendation.
criteria.below: Relies on jargon or acronyms without explaining them, or the order of ideas is hard to follow.
criteria.little: Communication is confusing, disorganized or mostly technical terms the owner cannot follow.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the cloud system, bank feeds and POS integration to faster closes that meet the bank's 15 day deadline, and weighs the $1,400 saving against internet dependence and conversion effort.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the cost exhibit and the owner's problems to the choice of the cloud system.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how the system change affects the bank deadline.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives a clear decision to switch to the cloud system with a practical plan: archive the old data, set up feeds and POS integration, start a backup and retention routine, and add multifactor authentication.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation to move to the cloud system supported by the $1,400 saving and added benefits.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or recommends keeping the current process unchanged.

criteria.exceeds: Presents the system uses, cost comparison, record preservation, data strategies and XBRL in plain language with a logical flow and confident, professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents all five topics clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips topics.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a simple side by side comparison ($6,800 against $5,400) or a before and after picture of the daily workflow, and adds practical ideas such as a monthly export backup or linking credit card and POS data.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the recommendation easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: choose an established provider, check the contract for data ownership and export rights, and export a full backup regularly (for example monthly) offsite; and bank feeds are generally read only and encrypted, so the software cannot move money, with multifactor authentication, limited administrator access and monthly bank reconciliation as safeguards.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that regular exported backups protect the data and that bank feeds are read only and secure.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague reassurance without specific safeguards.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or gives incorrect answers such as saying the cloud provider owns the data or that a bank feed lets the software move money.

key_points: Accounting software journalizes, posts to the general ledger and produces statements on demand, helping meet the bank's 15 day deadline
Cloud yearly cost = $450 x 12 = $5,400, a saving of $1,400 a year, plus remote access, automatic backups and bank feeds
Preserve records with the 3-2-1 backup rule, access levels and multifactor authentication, scanned receipts and retention periods (at least 3 years for tax, 4 years for payroll)
Export and archive a full copy of the old desktop data before switching
Data acquisition: bank and credit card feeds, POS integration, receipt capture apps and electronic vendor invoices, with imported data still reviewed
XBRL tags financial statement numbers so computers can read them; the SEC requires it for public companies, but RIVERSIDE HARDWARE is private and does not need it
